A bicycle, believed to be one of the Wright brothers’ bicycles, is on display at the National Museum of the United States Air Force.

When the Wright brothers started their flight research in Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903, bicycles were common transportation. At the time, bicycles typically used a single-speed chain driven by a single sprocket on the wheel. The sprocket had to be removed to remove the chain, and the wheel could not be turned.

In 1906, the Wrights began experimenting with bicycle-type chain drives in their airplane prototypes. They were so pleased with the results that they incorporated them into the airplanes. The bike drive allowed the airplane to be turned by placing the front sprocket in front of the pilot’s seat (which was on the same side as the rear sprocket). The front sprocket is connected by a chain to the rear sprocket, which is usually mounted on the propeller shaft.

original: For professors, publishing in elite journals is an unavoidable part of university life. The grueling process of subjecting work to the up-or-down judgment of credentialed scholarly peers has been a cornerstone of academic culture since at least the mid-20
sampled:
th century, when the first scholarly journals appeared. Today, a large portion of what we think of as “research” is actually the product of “research” published in one of these journals. In the humanities, where many students study works that have little bearing on day-to-day life, the journal publication process may seem like a needless form of credentialing, and one that is more about marketing than scholarship. In a recent article for The Atlantic, writer Matthew Yglesias calls for a moratorium on “scholarly” publication in journals that have little or no impact on academic life. He argues that the growing tendency for students to submit their research to these kinds of journals for publication has gone too far, and that the “journals aren’t just wrong, they’re fundamentally destructive.”

There’s no doubt that there are some journals that have become bloated, self-aggrandizing, and self-referential. Some of them have become gatekeepers, able to determine whether a work is worthy of academic study. And many of them have become too focused on marketing, and have little to do with rigorously assessing the quality of research.

DEAR T.D.: It would make sense for the lender to simply reimburse you for the difference. But that”s not how it works.

The lender should explain to you the different terms of your new loan. If you don”t agree to them, you can walk away from the loan before it closes — and likely lose the new house.

WASHINGTON - WASHINGTON (AP) — Federal regulators voted Wednesday to require companies to reveal more information about how they pay their executives amid a public outcry over compensation.
The Securities and Exchange Commission voted 4-to-1 to expand the disclosure requirements for
sampled:
"pay-for-performance" executive compensation, which includes stock options and other financial incentives.
The SEC, which operates independently from the Obama administration, says its new rules will force companies to report details about how they calculate pay and the benchmarks they set for executives.
"We are setting a new standard for the financial sector," said SEC Chairwoman Mary Jo White.
But some business groups and some Republican commissioners objected, saying the rules could raise compliance costs for companies and may limit their ability to offer stock options.
The new rules will require companies to report details about how they determine an executive's compensation, how they calculate the award, the weight that each factor will have in determining pay, the board's method of setting targets and the performance goals.
The SEC will require companies to issue so-called "pay-for-performance" proxy statements, which will be the first public disclosures companies will make about executive compensation. Companies will also have to file reports with the SEC on a quarterly basis.
The new rules are the SEC's latest attempt to rein in the rapid growth of executive compensation during the financial crisis.

But for the last decade, there’s been a movement in the world of food towards a simpler kind of eating: eating simply. It’s a term that gets thrown around a lot, but it basically boils down to eating food that is delicious and healthy, and eating food that is simple to prepare and eat.

Below, we’ll break down what simple eating is, and how you can incorporate it into your diet.

What Is Simple Eating

Simply put, simple eating is eating food that has healthy ingredients and low calories. This means that food that has a low calorie intake has fewer calories. It means that food that has low calorie content has fewer calories. It also means that food that is healthy has less carbs, less fat, less sugar, and so on.

While simple eating may seem like an oxymoron, these two things go hand in hand. The less processed the food, the less calories it will have, and the less calories you’ll eat. Low calorie is a good thing if you want to lose weight, but it’s often not enough on its own, so simple eating helps with that too.

As usual, Professor Jack Ponton (Letters, 8 July) cuts through all the smoke and mirrors erected by the renewables industries to give the facts.
He points out the absurdity of the regular and monotonous claims from the wind industry that
sampled:
wind produces more electricity than coal-fired stations. He provides figures that show that wind provides 2% of the UK's total electricity output, whereas coal-fired plants supply 26%.
Professor Ponton correctly notes that the UK's energy mix will change as renewables increase, but that the increase will be small and that such changes are necessary to meet future energy needs and ensure a secure energy supply.
He also notes that wind farms have a negative impact on view-lines for local people, wildlife and the landscape. These effects are exacerbated by the fact that wind turbines are not sited with a view to the local landscape.
Professor Ponton is right when he says that the UK has no choice but to reduce its use of coal, but the renewables industries do not have to provide all the power that is needed.
In addition, they should be forced to meet the conditions of planning permission that apply to other new developments, and the government should include them in the grid-turbine subsidy, which is currently reserved for onshore wind.
Richard Beale
Kettlewell, South Yorkshire
